title: Hooks on paper
description:
Work out the bytes a hooking library writes (lesson 4.04), for a function at a known address:

```cpp
struct InlineHook
{
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> patch;        // written over the start of the target function
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> trampoline;   // placed at the trampoline address
};

std::optional<InlineHook> planHook(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& functionStart, const std::vector<std::size_t>& lengths,
                                   std::uint64_t target, std::uint64_t hook, std::uint64_t trampolineAt);
std::uint64_t hookIat(std::vector<std::uint64_t>& iat, std::size_t slot, std::uint64_t replacement);
```

**planHook**: the target function starts at address `target`; `functionStart` holds its first bytes and `lengths` the lengths of its first instructions.
- Steal the fewest whole instructions covering at least 5 bytes. If they are not all available in `functionStart`, return `std::nullopt`.
- `patch` is an `E9` jump from `target` to `hook`, followed by `90`s to fill the rest of the stolen bytes.
- `trampoline` is the stolen bytes unchanged, then an `E9` jump from the end of those bytes (at `trampolineAt + stolen`) back to `target + stolen`.
- If a stolen instruction **starts** with a relative branch or call (`E8`, `E9`, `EB`, `70`-`7F`, `0F 80`-`0F 8F`), or any jump does not fit in 32 bits, return `std::nullopt`.

**hookIat** replaces the address in an import address table slot and returns the old one, so the hook can call the original.
hints: Find the stolen length first, checking each instruction as you add it. Then build both byte lists with one helper that appends an `E9` jump between two addresses and reports whether it fits.
lessonTitle: Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
